# **1\. Project overview** {#1.-project-overview}

## **1.1 Project Title** {#1.1-project-title}

AutoRestTest: An AI-Powered Platform for Automated REST API Testing 

## **1.2 Problem Statement** {#1.2-problem-statement}

As modern web services increasingly rely on REST APIs, ensuring their correctness is critical. As APIs grow in size and complexity, testing them becomes progressively harder because of large input spaces, interdependent operations, and the need for valid request sequences. Traditional automated testing tools often fail to explore these dependencies effectively, leading to low coverage, missed edge cases, and weak fault detection, while manual testing is time-consuming, repetitive, error-prone, and unable to scale with continuous development. Recent research such as AutoRestTest \[1\] shows that dependency-aware, reinforcement-learning and LLM-powered test generation can substantially improve coverage and fault detection for REST APIs. At the same time, development teams need a centralized, collaborative environment in which specifications, test suites, execution results, and reports can be stored, shared, and reused over time. Existing solutions rarely combine an intelligent testing engine with such a platform, and this gap is the problem this project addresses.

## **1.3 Objectives** {#1.3-objectives}

The main objectives of this project are as follows:

* To design and develop an AI-powered, collaborative SaaS platform for automated REST API testing, accessible through a centralized web dashboard.  
* To integrate an intelligent testing engine that uses dependency-aware, reinforcement-learning and LLM-based request generation, inspired by the AutoRestTest \[1\] approach, to maximize coverage and fault detection.  
* To allow users to upload OpenAPI specifications, or generate them with AI-assisted analysis, and to extract their endpoints automatically.  
* To automatically generate, save, and reuse test suites for each project.  
* To provide one-click, asynchronous test execution with real-time status updates and persistent execution history.  
* To present clear results and analytics, including status-code distribution, coverage, and server failures, together with LLM-based failure explanations and exportable PDF/CSV reports.  
* To enable secure team collaboration through project sharing and role-based access control.

## **1.4 Scope** {#1.4-scope}

The scope of this project defines the boundaries of the platform and the extent of the functionality it delivers. AutoRestTest is a web-based SaaS application for the functional testing of RESTful web services described by OpenAPI 3.0 specifications. Within this boundary it supports the complete testing workflow through a single centralized dashboard, from user and project management to specification handling, AI-driven test generation and execution, result analysis and reporting, and multi-user collaboration, so that development teams can automate REST API testing and reduce manual effort.

Certain areas are intentionally outside the scope of this project. The platform targets REST APIs only and does not address SOAP, GraphQL, or gRPC services, nor specification formats other than OpenAPI 3.0. It focuses on functional and fault-detection testing rather than load, stress, or performance testing, and it does not modify, deploy, or manage the systems under test. The platform further assumes that the target API is reachable over the network and that any credentials required to access protected endpoints are provided by the user.

## **1.5 Deliverables** {#1.5-deliverables}

The main deliverables of this project are as follows:

* A deployed web application (frontend and backend) that provides the AutoRestTest platform through a centralized, browser-based dashboard.  
* An AI-powered testing engine, deployed as an independent service, that performs dependency-aware, reinforcement-learning and LLM-based test generation and execution.  
* A PostgreSQL database implementing the platform's data model for users, projects, specifications, test suites, executions, results, and collaboration.  
* A complete, documented source-code repository covering the frontend, backend, and testing engine.  
* This technical report, documenting the project's overview, requirements, system and data models, AI engineering design, preliminary test plan and timeline.

# **2\. Requirements Analysis** {#2.-requirements-analysis}

## **2.1 Quality Function Deployment** {#2.1-quality-function-deployment}

### **2.1.1 Normal Requirements** {#2.1.1-normal-requirements}

Explicitly requested core features; user satisfaction is proportional to how well they are met.

#### **Functional Requirements** {#functional-requirements}

- [ ] **FR-N1 — User Authentication:** register, log in, and maintain secure sessions.  
- [ ] **FR-N2 — Project Management:** create, open, rename, and delete API testing projects from a central dashboard.  
- [ ] **FR-N3 — Specification Upload:** upload an OpenAPI 3.0 file; the system parses it and lists the extracted endpoints.  
- [ ] **FR-N4 — Test Execution:** run automated requests against the target API from a specification and collect the responses.  
- [ ] **FR-N5 — Result Viewing:** view each run's outcome per endpoint (method, request, response, status code, pass/fail).  
- [ ] **FR-N6 — Completion Notifications:** notify the user when a run completes, fails, or errors.

#### **Non-Functional Requirements** {#non-functional-requirements}

- [ ] **NFR-N1 — Usability:** the whole workflow is driven from one intuitive web dashboard, usable without special training.  
- [ ] **NFR-N2 — Responsiveness:** routine interactions (dashboard, navigation) load within a couple of seconds.

### **2.1.2 Expected Requirements** {#2.1.2-expected-requirements}

Implicitly assumed; their absence causes dissatisfaction even though users rarely ask for them by name.

#### **Functional Requirements** {#functional-requirements-1}

- [ ] **FR-E1 — Automatic Test Suite Generation:** automatically generate a comprehensive, dependency-aware suite of test cases from the specification.  
- [ ] **FR-E2 — Save & Reuse Suites:** persist named test suites for re-execution without reconfiguration.  
- [ ] **FR-E3 — Execution History:** keep every past run with its timestamp and outcome for later review.  
- [ ] **FR-E4 — Reports & Analytics:** per-run summary of HTTP status-code distribution, coverage, and server failures.  
- [ ] **FR-E5 — Export Reports:** download a run's results as PDF or CSV.  
- [ ] **FR-E6 — Team Collaboration:** invite members to a project and assign roles (admin, tester, viewer).

#### **Non-Functional Requirements** {#non-functional-requirements-1}

- [ ] **NFR-E1 — Security & Data Privacy:** passwords hashed, routes JWT-protected, and each user's and project's data isolated via role-based access control.  
- [ ] **NFR-E2 — Reliability:** long-running executions run asynchronously without blocking the UI and report status accurately.  
- [ ] **NFR-E3 — Data Persistence:** specifications, suites, runs, and results are stored durably and remain available across sessions.

### **2.1.3 Exciting Requirements** {#2.1.3-exciting-requirements}

Delighters beyond expectation; their absence isn't penalised, but their presence differentiates the platform. 

#### **Functional Requirements** {#functional-requirements-2}

- [ ] **FR-X1 — One-Click End-to-End Testing:** a single action runs the entire pipeline — read spec, generate tests, execute, and produce a report.  
- [ ] **FR-X2 — AI Failure Explanation:** LLM-generated, plain-language explanation of what caused a failure and which request triggered it.  
- [ ] **FR-X3 — AI Specification Generation:** automatically generate an OpenAPI specification from uploaded source code.

#### **Non-Functional Requirements** {#non-functional-requirements-2}

- [ ] **NFR-X1 — Extensibility:** the AI testing engine is deployed as an independent service, so its generation strategy can evolve without changing the web platform.

## **2.2 Stakeholders** {#2.2-stakeholders}

The key stakeholders of the platform and their interests are summarised below:

* API Developer: Uploads specifications and runs tests to catch defects in their REST APIs early.  
* QA Engineer / Tester: Generates and executes test suites and reviews results and failure explanations.  
* Team Lead / Project Manager: Creates projects, invites members, assigns roles, and tracks testing progress.  
* Viewer (Client / Stakeholder): Reviews reports and analytics without modifying tests.

## **2.3 Usage Scenario** {#2.3-usage-scenario}

### **2.3.1 Authentication System** {#2.3.1-authentication-system}

The system will have an authentication system with two options: sign up for new users and log in for users who already have an account.

**User Sign Up**  
A new user will begin registration by visiting the platform's sign-up page and clicking the Create Account button. The user will need to provide a valid email address, a username, and a password. The system will validate the uniqueness of the username and email and the format of the email address.

**User Login**  
Already registered users can log in by providing their email address and password on the login page. The system will maintain user sessions securely, allowing users to remain logged in without having to authenticate repeatedly. Users will also have the option to keep their login details saved for quicker access in future sessions.

### **2.3.2 Project Management** {#2.3.2-project-management}

Once logged in, users will be taken to the main dashboard where all their projects are displayed. The system will allow users to create, manage, and organise multiple API testing projects from a single centralised interface.

**Create Project**  
A user can create a new project by clicking the New Project button on the dashboard. The user will provide a project name and an optional description. Once created, the project will appear on the dashboard and the user will be taken to the project workspace where they can begin setting up their testing environment.

**Manage Projects**  
The dashboard will display all projects belonging to the user along with their names, creation dates, and last activity. Users can open, rename, or delete any project from the dashboard. Users can add multiple API endpoints inside a project. Deleting a project will remove all associated specifications, test suites, and results permanently, following a confirmation prompt from the system.

### **2.3.3 API Specification Management** {#2.3.3-api-specification-management}

Before testing can begin, users need to define the API they want to test. Each project may have an API specification. The system will provide two ways to do this: uploading an existing specification file or generating one automatically from source code.

**Upload OpenAPI Specification**  
Users can upload an OpenAPI specification file in .yaml format directly into their project. The system will parse and validate the uploaded file and display the list of detected API endpoints and operations, making them available for test generation. If the file contains errors or is not a valid specification, the system will notify the user with a description of the problem.

**Automated API Specification Generation**  
For users who do not have an existing specification file, the system will provide an option to generate one automatically. The user can upload their API source code files and the system will analyse them to produce a valid OpenAPI specification. The generated specification will be displayed for review before the user proceeds, and it can be used as the basis for testing in the same way as a manually uploaded file.

### **2.3.4 Test Suite Management** {#2.3.4-test-suite-management}

Once an API specification is available within the project, the system will allow users to generate, save, and reuse test suites for repeated testing.

**Automatic Test Suite Generation**  
After a specification is uploaded or generated, the system will automatically produce a comprehensive set of test cases covering the detected API endpoints and operations. The generated test suite will be displayed to the user showing each test case, its target endpoint, and the HTTP method that will be used. Users are not required to write or configure any test cases manually.

**Save and Reuse Test Suites**  
The test suite will be saved for future use. Saved test suites will appear in the project's Test Suites section and can be re-executed at any time without regenerating or reconfiguring them. This is particularly useful for regression testing, where the same suite needs to be run repeatedly after API changes.

### **2.3.5 Test Execution** {#2.3.5-test-execution}

When a test suite is executed, the system will send automated requests to the target API, collect the responses, and track the progress in real time.

**One-Click API Testing**  
The system will provide a single Run button that, when clicked, triggers the entire testing pipeline automatically. The system will read the active specification, generate test cases, execute all tests against the target API, and produce a full report — all without requiring any additional input from the user. This allows a team to run a complete API test in a single action.

**Running Tests**  
Users can initiate a test run by selecting a test suite and clicking the Run button. The system will display a live progress indicator showing which endpoints are currently being tested and how many have been completed. Users can monitor the execution as it progresses without needing to refresh the page.

**Test Alerts and Notifications**  
Once a test run is complete, the system will send the user a notification confirming completion along with a brief summary of the outcome. If the run encounters a failure — such as the target API being unreachable, an unexpected server error, or a system-level issue during execution — the user will be notified immediately with a description of what went wrong.

### **2.3.6 Test Results and Reports** {#2.3.6-test-results-and-reports}

After each test run, the system will store the results and provide detailed reporting and analysis options for the user to review.

**Viewing Test Results**  
Users can open any completed test run to see a full breakdown of the results. The results page will show each endpoint that was tested, the HTTP method used, the response received, and whether the test passed or failed. Users can filter the results by endpoint, response status, or HTTP response code to focus on specific areas of interest. In addition, the system records every individual request the engine sent during the run, so users can inspect the exact request and response captured for each call.

**Test Reports and Analytics**  
The system will generate a summary report for each completed test run showing the distribution of HTTP response codes received across all tested endpoints, any server-side failures that were detected, and the proportion of the API's endpoints that were covered during the run. This gives the team a complete picture of how the API performed.

**Test Failure Explanation**  
When a server-side failure or unexpected response is detected, the system will provide a plain-language explanation describing which request triggered the failure, what response was received, and what the likely cause may be. This reduces the time users spend investigating and diagnosing issues after a test run.

**Test Execution History**  
The system will maintain a complete history of all test runs for each project. Users can access the history from the project workspace and see a list of past executions with their timestamps, the test suite used, and a summary of outcomes. Any past run can be opened to review its full results in the same way as a recent run.

**Export Test Reports**  
Users can download the results and report of any completed test run in standard formats such as PDF or CSV. The exported file will contain the full results breakdown, the analytics summary, and the details of any detected failures, allowing users to share test outcomes with stakeholders or include them in project documentation.

### **2.3.7 Team Collaboration** {#2.3.7-team-collaboration}

The system will allow multiple users to collaborate within a shared project. The project owner can invite team members and assign them roles to control what each member can see and do within the project.

**Inviting Team Members**  
The project owner or an admin can invite other users to join the project by entering their email address. The invited user will receive an invitation with a link to accept it. Once accepted, the user will be added to the project and it will appear on their dashboard.

**Role Management**  
Each team member is assigned a role that determines their level of access. An admin can manage project settings, invite or remove members, and execute test runs. A tester can upload specifications, generate test suites, and run tests. A viewer can only see test results and reports without making any changes to the project. The project owner can update a member's role or remove them from the project at any time.

# **4\. Data Modeling** {#4.-data-modeling}

Database modeling describes how the platform's persistent data is structured and related. AutoRestTest uses a relational schema on **PostgreSQL**, accessed through the **Prisma** ORM. The model comprises nine entities and four enumerated types.

## **4.1 ER Diagram**  {#4.1-er-diagram}

Entity Relationships:

* A **User** can own many **Projects**.  
* A **User** can belong to many **Projects** through **ProjectMember**, a many-to-many association that carries the member's role (each row pairs one user with one project).  
* A **Project** can have many **ProjectInvitations**, and each invitation is sent by one **User**.  
* A **Project** has at most one **ApiSpecification**.  
* A **Project** contains many **Endpoints**.  
* A **Project** can have many **TestSuites**, and each **TestSuite** is triggered by one **User**.  
* A **TestSuite** produces many **TestCases**, and each **TestCase** tests one **Endpoint**.  
* A **TestSuite** captures many **RequestLogs**, and each **RequestLog** maps to at most one **Endpoint**.

![][image17]

*Figure 17: Entity Relationship Diagram*

# **5\. AI Engineering Design** {#5.-ai-engineering-design}

AutoRestTest concentrates its intelligence in the testing engine, which transforms a static API description into an adaptive testing process. Rather than treating operation selection, dependency resolution, parameter selection, and value generation as isolated, one-off steps, the engine coordinates them as a single learning system that combines a semantic dependency graph, Large-Language-Model (LLM) value generation, and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL).

## **5.1 AI Pipeline** {#5.1-ai-pipeline}

The AI pipeline turns the target service's OpenAPI description into concrete test requests and refines its own strategy from every server response. As shown in Figure 18, it operates in two phases: an initialization phase that prepares the search space, and an iterative testing-execution phase that explores it within a fixed time budget.

**Initialization phase:** The pipeline begins by parsing the target service's OpenAPI 3.0 specification, extracting every operation together with its parameters and request/response schemas. From these operations it constructs the Semantic Property Dependency Graph (SPDG) — a directed graph in which each node is an API operation and each edge represents a potential data dependency between two operations. Edges are weighted by the cosine similarity between the names of one operation's output properties and another's input properties, so that operations likely to feed one another (for example, a “create user” call that produces an identifier later consumed by a “get user” call) are linked with a high initial weight. This lets the tool prioritise plausible dependencies instead of blindly matching every input against every output. Finally, the reinforcement-learning agents are created, each with its own Q-table mapping the choices it can make to their expected reward. During this phase the Value Agent also pre-generates realistic, context-aware values by querying the LLM with few-shot prompts in JSON mode; because this step is not part of the time-bounded loop, it can be performed ahead of testing and cached.

**Testing-execution phase:** Testing then runs as an iterative loop driven by four cooperating agents, each responsible for a single decision:  
**Operation Agent** — selects the next API operation to exercise.  
**Parameter Agent** — chooses which combination of parameters to include.

**Value Agent** — generates a value for each parameter, choosing the most effective data source: an LLM-generated value, a value carried over from a dependent operation, or a type-based default.  
**Dependency Agent** — supplies values drawn from previously successful operations, guided by the SPDG.  
In the implementation, the Value Agent's responsibilities are further divided across dedicated value, data-source, and request-body agents, with an optional header agent for authenticated targets; the four roles above capture the core decision structure.

**Request generation and mutation:** On each iteration, the Request Generator assembles a concrete HTTP request from the chosen operation, parameters, values, and headers. A Mutator then perturbs roughly 20% of requests — altering values, types, headers, or methods — specifically to probe error handling and surface faults that valid requests would never reveal. The request is dispatched to the Service Under Test (SUT), and its response is captured and analysed: successful (2xx) responses yield values that are cached for reuse in later requests, while internal server errors (5xx) are recorded for the final report.

**The learning loop:** The response is the reward signal that closes the loop. Every agent's Q-table is updated using value-decomposition Q-learning with a temporal-difference update, which distributes a shared reward across the agents so that each converges toward its best action while accounting for the others' choices. Action selection follows an ε-greedy strategy in which the exploration rate decays over the run — from broad exploration early on to focused exploitation later — balancing the discovery of new behaviours against the reuse of proven ones. In parallel, the SPDG is refined: edge weights are increased for dependencies confirmed by successful responses, decreased for those that fail, and edges that fall below a threshold are pruned, so the dependency model grows more accurate as testing progresses. This cycle repeats until the configured time budget is exhausted, after which the pipeline emits the testing report summarising tested operations, code and operation coverage, the status-code distribution, detected 500-level server errors, and the full execution history.

Because each component addresses a different source of difficulty — the SPDG narrows the dependency search space, the LLM produces domain-realistic inputs, and MARL coordinates the testing strategy over time — they are complementary: the pipeline achieves broader coverage and detects more faults than approaches that optimise any one of these steps in isolation.

![][image18]

*Figure 18: AI system workflow diagram*

## **5.2 Model Selection** {#5.2-model-selection}

AutoRestTest does not depend on any single language model. Because the testing engine communicates with the LLM through a standard OpenAI-compatible REST API, the user is free to choose whichever model best suits their budget and accuracy needs, provided it meets three conditions: it is reachable through an OpenAI-compatible API, it supports structured JSON output (JSON mode), and it is capable of interpreting OpenAPI specifications to generate valid, context-aware request data. Suitable models include OpenAI's GPT family and open-weight models such as gpt-oss-20b (used by default via OpenRouter); other providers such as Google Gemini can also be used when accessed through an OpenAI-compatibility endpoint. The selected model is set in a single configuration entry, so switching models — for example, moving from a free open-weight model during development to a stronger frontier model for higher-fidelity value generation — requires only a configuration change and no modification to the engine.

## **5.3 Prompt Design** {#5.3-prompt-design}

The engine relies on carefully engineered prompts to drive its LLM interactions. Rather than one general prompt, it uses a family of task-specific prompts that share a few common design principles: each injects the operation summary together with its OpenAPI schema, instructs the model to return a strict JSON structure (paired with the model's JSON mode), and supplies few-shot examples so the output matches the expected format. These prompts fall into four groups: 

* Value-generation prompts: produce valid, context-aware values for an operation's parameters and request body.   
* Feedback / retry prompts: regenerate values after a failed request by conditioning on the server's response, dropping inputs that caused the failure.   
* Classification prompts: label failures (for example, parameter-constraint, format, or dependency errors) so the engine can respond appropriately.   
* Utility prompts: handle supporting tasks such as repairing malformed JSON and identifying authentication parameters.

Here is some example:

**CLASSIFICATION\_PROMPT** \= ''' Given an error message, classify the error as one of "PARAMETER CONSTRAINT, FORMAT, PARAMETER DEPENDENCY, OPERATION DEPENDENCY". '''

**REQUEST\_BODY\_GEN\_PROMPT** \= """ Given a summary of an operation its request body schema from its OpenAPI Specification, generate a valid context-aware request body for the operation. Return the answer as a JSON object with the following structure: { "request\_body": \[correct request body\] } In the case where the request body is an object, return a correctly formatted object as the \[correct request body\] value. In the object, include all required fields as specified from the OpenAPI Specification for object request bodies, but otherwise include/exclude optional properties to ensure the object is accepted. In the case where the request body is an array, use a list as the request\_body value. Do not solely rely on the given constraint values, and ensure you read the associated descriptions for maximum accuracy. Use any provided example values to guide your generation formatting."""

**IDENTIFY\_AUTHENTICATION\_SYSTEM\_MESSAGE** \= "You will receive a summary of an operation and its full schema from the OpenAPI Specification. Your goal is to determine if the operation consists of any authentication information sent as parameters in either the query or the request body. When referring to request body parameters, identify object properties that might be used for authentication. Authentication information specifically refers to either usernames or passwords (or similar). Return your result in the specified JSON format."

# **6\. User Manual & User Interface** {#6.-user-manual-&-user-interface}

## **6.1 Introduction** {#6.1-introduction}

AutoRestTest is a web-based, AI-powered, collaborative platform for automated REST API testing. It brings together several capabilities that are normally spread across separate tools into a single project workspace:

* **API specification management:** Upload an existing OAS (OpenAPI Specification) document in .json or .yaml format, or generate one automatically by uploading a zip of the API's source code.  
* **Dependency visualization:** a semantic dependency graph shows which API operations rely on data produced by other operations, before a single request is ever sent.  
* **AI-driven test execution:** a multi-agent reinforcement-learning and LLM-backed engine generates and runs a test suite against a live target API, with real-time status and a detailed report.  
* **Team collaboration:** invite teammates to a project with a specific role (Admin, Tester, or Viewer) and work together on the same specification, endpoints, and test runs.

This manual walks through every page and feature of the application, in the order a new user would typically encounter them, so that any user regardless of technical background can get started quickly.

## **6.2 System Requirements** {#6.2-system-requirements}

* A modern web browser (Google Chrome, Firefox, Microsoft Edge, or Safari).  
* An internet connection.  
* An AutoRestTest account (registered through the application itself).  
* For AI powered API specification generation from source code: the source code packaged as a single .zip archive, up to 50 MB.

No installation is required on the user's computer. The entire platform runs in the browser.

## **6.3 Accessing AutoRestTest** {#6.3-accessing-autoresttest}

Open your browser and navigate to the AutoRestTest URL provided to you. If you are not already signed in, the application takes you to the Landing page.

![][image19]  
       *Figure 19: AutoRestTest Landing Page*

## **6.4 Creating an Account** {#6.4-creating-an-account}

**6.4.1 Registering**

If you do not already have an account, you can create one from the Register page.

1\.      On the Landing page, click "Sign Up" on the right side of the top navigation row.  
2\.      Fill in the registration form:

* **Username:** a unique name, 3–32 characters. This becomes your permanent sign-in name and cannot be changed later.  
* **Email:** a valid email address you have access to. This also becomes your permanent email address.  
* **Password:** at least 8 characters.

3\.      Click "Create account".

Registration does not create your account immediately, it only reserves it. AutoRestTest sends a six-digit verification code to the email address you entered, and you are taken to the Confirm Your Email screen.

                      ![][image20]    

                                    *Figure 20: Account register page*

**6.4.2 Verifying Your Email**

The Confirm Your Email screen shows six input boxes for the six-digit code that was emailed to you. Typing (or pasting) the code fills the boxes automatically and, once all six digits are entered, the form submits itself, there is no separate button to click. Your account is only created at this step, once the code is verified.

* If you did not receive the code, use the "Resend the code" link. Once used, it is disabled for 60 seconds before it can be used again.  
* If you entered the wrong email address, use the "Sign up again" link to restart registration.

On success you are signed in automatically and taken straight to your Projects page. There is no separate account-approval step and no unverified state to wait out.

                    ![][image21]

                                             *Figure 21: Email verification page*

## **6.5 Logging In** {#6.5-logging-in}

1. On the Login page, enter your Email or username and your Password in a single combined field for the identifier. Either your email address or your username is accepted.  
2. Click "Sign in".  
3. If your credentials are correct, you are taken directly into the application, on your Projects page.

                       *![][image22]*

                                                *Figure 22: Login page*

**6.5.1 Forgot Password**

If you have forgotten your password, click "Forgot your password?" on the Login page.

1. Enter the email address on your account and click "Send reset link".  
2. Check your inbox for a reset link. For security, the screen shows the same confirmation message whether or not the address is registered, so it cannot be used to discover which emails have an account.  
3. The link works once and expires after 30 minutes.  
4. Opening the link takes you to the Choose a New Password screen, where you enter and confirm a new password (at least 8 characters, and the two entries must match).

Resetting your password signs you out of every device and browser you were previously signed in on, including the one you are using now. Sign in again with your new password.

## **![][image23] ![][image24]**

                                            *Figure 23: Reset password page*

## **6.6 The Application Layout** {#6.6-the-application-layout}

After signing in, the application uses a single top bar for all navigation — there is no sidebar. From left to right, the top bar contains:

* **AutoRestTest logo,** which always returns to your Projects list.  
* **Project switcher,** visible whenever you are inside a project; shows the current project's name and lets you jump directly to any other project without returning to the list first.  
* **Invitations bell icon,** shown only when you have at least one pending project invitation, with a badge showing how many.  
* Your display name, and a light/dark theme toggle.  
* **Account menu,** opened from your avatar, with links to "Invitations", "Settings", and "Sign out".

![][image25]

                                            *Figure 24: Navbar*

## **6.7 Projects** {#6.7-projects}

The Projects page is what you see immediately after signing in. It is the application's home page. Each project is an independent workspace holding one API specification, its endpoints, its dependency graph, its test runs, and its team.

**6.7.1 Viewing Your Projects**

The Projects page offers:

* **A search box,** which filters by project name or description.  
* **A role filter,** with options All roles, Owner, Admin, Tester, and Viewer.  
* **A view toggle,** switching between a Table view and a Cards view; your choice is remembered for next time.

The table view's columns such as Name, Members, Role, and Last activity can each be clicked to sort the list; clicking the same column again reverses the sort order. A Status column shows badges for the project's specification state (No spec / Spec uploaded / Spec generated), any AI generation in progress (Generating… / Awaiting review / Generation failed), and the status of its most recent test run.

![][image26]

                            *Figure 25: Homepage dashboard page*

**6.7.2 Creating a Project**

1\.   Click "+ New Project".  
2\.   Enter a Name (required) and, optionally, a Description.  
3\.   Click "Create project".

You are taken directly into the new project, on its Overview tab.

                   ![][image27]

                                         *Figure 26: Create new project form*

**6.7.3 Editing or Deleting a Project**

Only a project's owner can edit or delete it. From the project's own page, use the Edit and Delete buttons next to the project name; from the Projects list, open the row menu on a project you own. Deleting a project asks for confirmation and permanently removes the project and everything in it such as its specification, endpoints, dependency graph, test runs, and captured requests.

## **6.8 Project Roles and Permissions** {#6.8-project-roles-and-permissions}

Every project has one owner and any number of members, each holding one of three roles. Permissions are enforced both in the interface and on the server.

| Role | Can do |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Owner** | Everything below, plus rename or delete the project itself, and manage all members. |
| **Admin** | Manage the API specification and endpoints; configure, run, and manage test suites; manage team members and invitations. |
| **Tester** | Configure and trigger test runs; run individual captured or live requests. Cannot change the specification, endpoints, or team. |
| **Viewer** | Read-only access to everything in the project; cannot change or run anything. |

 

## **6.9 Project Overview Tab** {#6.9-project-overview-tab}

Opening a project lands on its Overview tab. A tab row beneath the project name shows Overview, API Spec, Endpoints, Dependencies, Test Suites, Team; switches between the project's sections; it stays visible throughout.

The Overview tab shows the project's description, its owner, member count, creation date, and last-updated date, alongside a short list of its team (owner and members, each with a role badge).

![][image28]

                                             *Figure 27: Project overview*

## **6.10 API Specification** {#6.10-api-specification}

The API Spec tab is where a project's OpenAPI document lives. Project owners and admins are offered two ways to provide one, selected with a toggle at the top of the page: Upload OAS file, or Generate from source code. Testers and viewers see only the specification that is currently in place.  
**6.10.1 Uploading an OpenAPI File**

1\.   Select "Upload OAS file".  
2\.   Drag an OpenAPI document onto the drop zone, or click it to browse for a file. Accepted formats are .json, .yaml, and .yml, describing an OpenAPI 3.x document.

Endpoints are extracted automatically as soon as the file is accepted. If the project already has a specification, uploading a new one asks for confirmation first, since replacing it re-extracts the endpoint list and removes any endpoints that were added manually.

Once a specification is in place, its card shows the document's title, its OpenAPI version, an AI-generated badge if it came from the code-generation flow described below, its endpoint count, and its upload date along with Replace and Delete buttons. The raw specification text is shown below, with buttons to copy it or download it as a file.

![][image29]

                                                   *Figure 28: API Specification management*

**6.10.2 Generating a Specification from Source Code**

If a project does not yet have an OpenAPI specification, AutoRestTest can generate one automatically by reading the API's own source code with an AI pipeline.

1. Select "Generate from source code".  
2. Fill in the API title and Version (both prefilled from the project's own name and "1.0.0"), and, optionally, adjust Exclude directories by a comma-separated list of folders to skip (vendored dependencies and build output are pre-filled, since excluding them makes the analysis considerably faster and cheaper).  
3. Drag the project's source code onto the drop zone as a single .zip archive (up to 50 MB), or click to browse for one.

Generation runs in the background and can take a long time for a large codebase. The page shows a progress bar, the current step, and an elapsed-time counter, and updates automatically, so it is safe to leave the page and come back later. A "Cancel" button discards a generation that is still running.

![][image30]  
                                          *Figure 29: Auto generate API Specification* 

Once generation finishes, the specification is shown for review before it changes anything in the project. Any warnings from the pipeline; for example, a note that a required tool was unavailable and a lower-fidelity conversion was used are shown alongside it. Clicking "Review generated spec" expands the full generated document. From here you can either "Discard" the result, or click "Use this specification" to apply it as the project's specification (if one already existed, this asks for confirmation first, for the same reason as replacing an uploaded file).

## **6.11 Endpoints** {#6.11-endpoints}

The Endpoints tab lists every operation extracted from the project's specification, plus any added manually. A search box filters by path, method, or description.

Each row shows:

* An HTTP method badge (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, …).  
* The endpoint's path, with inline indicators for whether authentication is required, how many parameters it takes, and whether it accepts a request body.  
* Its description.  
* A Source badge "From spec" for endpoints extracted from the uploaded or generated specification, or "Manual" for ones added by hand.

Clicking a row expands its full detail directly beneath it: authentication requirements, every parameter (with where it is sent, path, query, header, or cookie, its type, and whether it is required), the request body schema with an example payload, and the documented responses.

![][image31]  
                                                     *Figure 30: API Endpoints*

Project owners and admins can add an endpoint manually with "+ Add endpoint"; choosing a Method, entering a Path, and optionally a Description for cases the specification does not cover. Manual endpoints can also be deleted from the row menu.

                         ![][image32]  
                                        *Figure 31: Add API Endpoint manually*

## **6.12 Dependency Graph** {#6.12-dependency-graph}

The Dependencies tab visualizes the Semantic Property Dependency Graph the engine builds from the specification: an edge from one operation to another means the first operation is believed to produce a value the second one needs; for example, an edge from "create a resource" to "fetch that resource by id" because the id one returns is what the other expects as input. Building the graph only reads the specification; it never sends any request to the API itself.

* Click "Build dependency graph" (available to admins and testers; viewers ask a teammate with one of those roles to do it). This takes roughly a minute, since the engine compares every operation against every other one.  
*  Once built, the graph can be rebuilt at any time from the same tab.

![][image33]  
                                                      *Figure 32: SPDG Visualization*

## **6.13 Test Suites** {#6.13-test-suites}

The Test Suites tab is where AI-generated test runs are configured, executed, and reviewed. Each entry in its table is one run: its name (or a short generated id), status, target URL, pass/total result once complete, and creation date.  
**6.13.1 Creating a New Run**

1. Click "+ New run".  
2. Optionally give the run a Name.  
3.  Enter the Target URL; the live base URL the engine will send requests to.  
4. Set the Time budget in seconds (default 300); how long the AI engine is allowed to spend generating and sending requests.  
5. Optionally set a Mutation rate between 0 and 1, controlling how aggressively the engine varies generated values.  
6. An "Advanced: Custom headers" section can be expanded to attach up to 20 HTTP headers to every request the run sends; for example an Authorization header for Basic or Bearer authentication, or an API-key header the target API expects. Each row is a free-form key and value; common header names are suggested as you type.  
7. Click "Create" to save the run.

A newly created run starts in the Pending state and has not sent any requests yet.  
 ![][image34]  
                                            *Figure 32: Create test suite*  
**6.13.2 Running and Monitoring a Test Run**  
Open a pending run and click "Run tests" to start it. While running, the page polls automatically every few seconds and needs no manual refresh. A run can end in one of four states:

| Status | Meaning |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Pending** | Configured, but not yet started. |
| **Running** | The AI engine is actively generating and sending requests to the target. |
| **Completed** | The run finished and produced a report. |
| **Failed** | The run could not be completed. For example because the target URL was unreachable or the engine service was unavailable. It can be retried. |

**6.13.3 Viewing the Test Report**  
Once a run completes, its page shows a full report. A run's job is finding real defects, not just checking for a non-2xx response: a request that receives a 4xx means the API correctly rejected a bad request, while a 5xx server error is the genuine fault signal. The headline banner reflects this directly, reporting the number of faults (5xx responses) detected, or confirming that none were found.  
Below the banner:

* A KPI row shows coverage percentage, endpoints covered, total requests sent, and the breakdown of successful (2xx), client-error (4xx), and server-error (5xx) responses.  
* A status-code distribution chart shows the same breakdown visually.  
* A per-endpoint results table lists every endpoint the run exercised, with a Result badge (Successful / Client error / Server error), the exact status codes returned, and any failure explanation generated for it. It can be filtered by search term, outcome, or exact status code.  
* For a completed run whose report has failures, an "Explain failures" button asks the AI engine to generate a plain-language explanation of what likely caused each failure and which request triggered it.  
* The same dependency graph described in section 1.12 is shown again here, scoped to this run — which lets you see exactly which dependencies the reinforcement-learning agent confirmed while generating this particular run's requests.

![][image35]  
                                               *Figure 32: Test report*

**6.13.4 Exporting Reports**  
A completed run offers "Export CSV" and "Export PDF" buttons, each of which downloads the run's report in that format for sharing outside the application.  
**6.13.5 Replaying a Run**  
A completed run can be replayed with the "Replay" button: this resends that run's exact captured requests, in the same order, as a new, separate run — with no new AI generation involved. This is useful for confirming whether a fix actually resolved a previously-detected fault, since it is an apples-to-apples comparison against the same requests. A run's page shows a Run History panel listing its original run and every replay of it, so results can be compared side by side.

## **6.14 Captured Requests and Live Request Runs** {#6.14-captured-requests-and-live-request-runs}

From a completed run's report, clicking "View all captured requests" — or "View" next to a specific endpoint, or a node in the run's dependency graph — opens the full list of every request the engine actually sent during that run. The list can be filtered by endpoint and by response status class (2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx) or an exact status code, and is paginated 50 rows at a time.

Expanding a request shows the complete exchange: the request's method, URL, headers, and body on one side, and the response's status, duration, headers, and body on the other. A "Copy as curl" button builds a ready-to-run curl command from the captured request.

A "Run" button lets an admin or tester resend that exact request to the target API right now, and shows the fresh response inline as a Live response, without leaving the page. Because a non-GET/HEAD request can have real side effects on the target system, running anything other than a GET or HEAD request asks for confirmation first.

The Team tab (and the shorter team list on the Overview tab) shows everyone with access to the project: the owner, then every other member with their role. Owners and admins can change another member's role (Admin, Tester, or Viewer) directly from a dropdown next to their name, or remove them from the project with "Remove". Any member can leave a project they no longer need access to with "Leave".

3\.   Click "Send invite".  
The invitation is emailed to that address. Pending invitations are listed on the Team tab with their role, expiry date, and status; each can be resent, have its invite token copied, or be revoked before it is accepted.

**6.15.3 My Invitations**

## **6.16 Account Settings** {#6.16-account-settings}

The Settings page, reached from the account menu, is organized into four sections.

**6.16.1 Profile**  
Lets you choose an avatar colour and set an optional Display name. Your Username and Email are shown read-only — the username is what you sign in with and cannot be changed, and every account on the platform is always verified, so no separate verification badge or step applies here. Click "Save changes" once you have made an edit.

**6.16.2 Password**  
Lets you change your password by entering your Current password and a New password (entered twice to confirm). Changing your password signs you out of every device, including the one you used to change it — you will need to sign in again with the new password.

**6.16.3 Notifications**  
Two checkboxes control optional email notifications and are saved the instant you toggle them: "Test run finished" (an email when a run you started completes or fails) and "Project invitations" (an email when someone invites you to a project — invitations still appear inside the application either way). Security emails — verification codes, password-reset links, and password-change confirmations — are always sent and cannot be turned off.

**6.16.4 Deleting Your Account**  
The Danger Zone section offers "Delete my account". Since deleting your account also deletes every project you own — along with its specification, test runs, and captured requests, and removes your teammates' access to them — the confirmation dialog states exactly how many owned projects will be lost, and requires your current password before proceeding. This action cannot be undone.

To end your session, open the account menu from your avatar in the top bar and click "Sign out". You are returned to the Login page.

## **6.18 Frequently Asked Questions** {#6.18-frequently-asked-questions}

**Q:** I registered but never got my six-digit code. What should I do?  
**A:** Use the "Resend the code" link on the verification screen — it is available again 60 seconds after the previous send. If the address was mistyped, use "Sign up again" to restart with the correct one.

**Q:** Why can't I change my username?  
**A:** A username is the identity you sign in with, so AutoRestTest treats it as permanent once an account is created. You can still set a separate Display name in Settings, which is what teammates see around the app.

**Q:** Generating a specification from my source code is taking a very long time. Is something wrong?  
**A:** Not necessarily. The pipeline reads your source code and calls an AI model to infer the specification, and large codebases can take a long time end-to-end. The page updates automatically, so it is safe to leave and come back later. Excluding vendored and build directories in the Exclude directories field before starting makes it noticeably faster.

**Q:** My completed run shows some 4xx responses. Is that a failure?  
**A:** Not on its own. AutoRestTest treats a 4xx response as the API correctly rejecting a request it considered invalid — it is only counted as a fault when the API returns a 5xx server error, which indicates the API failed to handle the request at all.

**Q:** What is the difference between rebuilding a run and replaying it?  
**A:** Re-running a pending run for the first time uses the AI engine to generate new requests. "Replay", available on a completed run, instead resends that exact same set of previously captured requests, in the same order, as a new run with no new generation — useful for confirming whether a fix actually resolved a fault.

**Q:** I accidentally deleted a project, a test run, or an endpoint. Can I get it back?  
**A:** No. Every delete in AutoRestTest is permanent and cannot be undone, which is why each one asks for confirmation first. Make sure you mean to delete something before confirming.

**Q:** Can I invite someone who doesn't have an AutoRestTest account yet?  
**A:** Yes. An invitation is sent to an email address, not an existing account; the recipient can register (or sign in, if they already have an account under that address) and then find the invitation waiting on their own "Invitations" page.

**Q:** Why is the "Run" button disabled on a captured request?  
**A:** Resending a live request is limited to project Admins and Testers. Viewers can see every captured request but cannot trigger new ones against the live target API.

# **7\. Test Report** {#7.-test-report}

## **7.1 Testing Strategy Overview** {#7.1-testing-strategy-overview}
To ensure the reliability, architectural integrity, data security, and operational correctness of AutoRestTest, a comprehensive two-tier testing methodology was established and executed throughout the development lifecycle:
1. **Automated Unit & Component Testing:** Continuous, test-driven verification targeting the isolated logic of services, controllers, guards, algorithms, and microservice runners across both the application backend and the AI engine service.
2. **System & Black-Box Acceptance Testing:** Scenario-driven end-to-end testing across 7 functional modules, validating real-world workflows, permission boundaries, asynchronous states, and failure recovery on the deployed platform.

Across both tiers, a total of **352 tests** (302 automated unit tests and 50 system test cases) were executed, achieving a **100% pass rate** with zero defects or regressions.

---

## **7.2 Automated Unit Testing** {#7.2-automated-unit-testing}
Automated unit testing forms the backbone of the platform's verification, guaranteeing that regressions are caught immediately during development and continuous integration.
